newsitem.title: NORWAY: US, Norway and Russia sign nuclear waste pact.
newsitem.headline: US, Norway and Russia sign nuclear waste pact.

text.p: The United States, Russia and Norway signed a landmark agreement on Thursday for the joint handling of nuclear wastes from scrapped Cold War submarines piling up on Russia's barren Kola peninsula.

The Arctic Military and Environmental Cooperation (AMEC) pact includes projects for development of containers for interim storage of spent nuclear fuel and work on technology for treatment of liquid as well as solid radioactive waste.
The agreement also addresses the dumping of whole nuclear reactors in the sea mainly during the Communist era.

AMEC was signed by U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and Norwegian counterpart Joergen Kosmo on the fringes of a NATO meeting in the Norwegian west coast city of Bergen.

"There is a greater benefit from doing this work together," Perry told a news conference after the three shook hands and toasted in champagne. "We are also bridging the Cold War chasms and building new security relationships based on trust and cooperation."

U.S. officials said it would be the first time that U.S. military visit former Soviet submarine bases in Murmansk and other ports on the Kola peninsula, whose strategic nuclear arsenals formed the backbone of the Communist superpower's military deterrence. An initial planning meeting will be held in Murmansk, but a date has yet to be set.

Norwegian experts say the Kola peninsula has the highest concentration in the world of nuclear reactors, active or derelict. The Cold War arms race went too fast for Soviet authorities to plan for what to do with decommissioned submarines and the nuclear waste. Arms reduction agreements have added to the environmental problems on the barren peninsula.
"Considerable numbers of nuclear-powered submarines were withdrawn from the strength of our navy as a result of arms reduction," Rodionov said.

"It is not a simple work to carry out. We need to offload nuclear fuel from reactors and we also need to keep it at the military installation and that poses a considerable risk for the environment," he said.

Russia has more than 80 operational nuclear submarines and two nuclear-powered cruisers stationed at bases on the Kola. In addition, at least 70 nuclear submarines have been scrapped, but spent nuclear fuel has been removed from only about 20, partly because of a lack of storage sites, Norway says.
Storage sites for spent fuel and other nuclear waste from vessels scrapped under disarmament agreements are inadequate and radiation could leak into the Barents Sea, experts say.

NATO member Norway, which shares a 200 km (125 miles) Arctic frontier with Russia, has pushed hard for the agreement as part of efforts to draw international attention to the environmental hazards on the neighbouring peninsula.
In its first year, AMEC has a budget of two million dollars to be divided up among the three nations, but costs will rise as altogether six projects take off, U.S. officials said.

Nils Boehmer, a physicist with the Norwegian environmental group Bellona, which is sponsored partly by the government, said AMEC was a step in the right direction but that it failed to address the issue of spent nuclear fuel properly.
"That is the main problem," he said. "How to handle spent highly radioactive nuclear fuel from submarines."
Boehmer said a prototype container for spent nuclear fuel being planned under AMEC would only handle the waste of one of many reactors.

"Secondly, the agreement does not leave any room for civilian inspection," he said. "The civilian radiation authorities in Norway, Russia and the United States are being kept out. We fear information will be kept away from the public."
